newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers expect lawsuits in TWA crash to multiply.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers expect lawsuits in TWA crash to multiply.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent

Lawsuits in the deadly TWA Flight 800 crash will begin to multiply this week after the National Transportation and Safety Board said a fuel tank problem could have caused the explosion, lawyers said on Monday.

Lee Kreindler of New York's Kreindler & Kreindler said he expected to file more cases this week in addition to the 19 he has already brought against TWA and Boeing Co alleging the explosion was caused by a mechanical malfunction. The suits, filed in federal courts in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Philadelphia, also ask that the defendants be held liable if it is found the explosion was caused by a bomb.

"I think the whole thing is very gratifying," Kreindler said of the NTSB statement. "We have been saying from day one that this was mechanical, structural, electrical failure leading to an explosion in the fuel tank.

"The board is right where they should be. They're right in the central fuel tank as the start of the whole process ... It's within the sphere of responsibility of the manufacturer and the airline. It's becoming a very strong, very powerful products liability case."

Kreindler, whose firm represents 39 families, said he was unsure how many cases would be filed this week. He is also the lead plaintiffs' counsel in litigation involving the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie.
Although other plaintiffs' lawyers criticised Kreindler, saying he acted prematurely in a bid for publicity when he filed his first suits in October, they are now also suing TWA and Boeing.

One of those lawyers, Kenneth Nolan of Speiser, Krause, Madole & Nolan, said his firm filed one case last week in state court in Brooklyn and expected to file more cases in the next few weeks. His firm represents seven families.

"We feel that essentially the NTSB and FBI have ruled out a bomb or a missile so that only leaves mechanical. The centre fuel tank exploded. You're dealing with an ageing airplane. We feel confident they will eventually come out and say it's mechanical failure," Nolan said.
In addition to the litigation, families of victims of the explosion pressed TWA for immediate compensation.
Families of crash victims met with TWA on Monday to try and get money for financially pressed families who lost a main breadwinner in the crash.
"We feel progress has been made," said Jose Cremades, a spokesman for the group. He said the families looked forward to continuing talks with the airline but offered few other details on the issue.

The NTSB on Friday said a buildup of volatile vapours in the 747's partially full centre fuel tank could have triggered the July 17 explosion that killed all 230 people aboard and it issued urgent recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration to act to prevent future such disasters. But it stopped short of blaming the crash of the New York-to-Paris flight on mechanical failure, a bomb or a missile
The FAA said it would urgently review the recommendations. Boeing said it would comply with any FAA directives issued.

The NTSB statement has drawn criticism from other investigators searching for the cause of the explosion. James Kallstrom, head of the FBI's New York office, took issue with safety board speculation that static electricity caused the explosion, saying through a spokesman it was not helpful for investigators to speculate about the cause of the crash.

The New York Times reported on Monday that a senior NTSB investigator said he and other agency investigators involved in the wreckage analysis were surprised and disturbed by the board's statement identifying a possible cause for the crash.
